chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who said to his wife, 'You are free from me,' or 'disavowed from me,' or 'severed,' or 'prohibited.' He said: 'It is not anything (i.e., it does not constitute a formal divorce).'

key_terms.حَرَامٌ: Prohibited; indicating the wife is now forbidden to him.
key_terms.خَلِيَّةٌ: Free/disengaged; a term used phrase for divorce.
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِشَيْءٍ: It is nothing; a legal ruling meaning no divorce has occurred.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a husband saying 'you are free from me' to his wife?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that common verbal declarations such as 'you are free' or 'you are prohibited from me' do not constitute a formal divorce (*talaq*) unless accompanied by specific intent or formula. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle of distinguishing between explicit divorce terms and general expressions of separation, emphasizing that mere words without clear intent or technical precision do not sever the marital bond.
